title: In-Training Compression of State Space Models
one_liner: Growing a large state space model and shrinking it during training preserves task structure while cutting compute costs.
lead: State Space Models are a type of machine learning model designed to process long sequences of data, like stock prices or sensor readings over time. To work well, these models need to remember a lot of information in their hidden state (the internal numbers they use to process each new input). But a larger hidden state means more computation and slower training. This paper shows that if you start with a large model and gradually remove unimportant hidden state dimensions during training, you end up with a smaller model that is faster to train and performs better than if you had trained a small model from the start, because the early large state lets the model discover all the patterns it needs, then pruning removes only the dimensions that were never used.

problem.h2: The tradeoff between memory and speed
paras: State Space Models work by keeping track of a hidden state (a list of numbers that represents what the model has learned so far) and updating it for each new piece of data. The bigger this hidden state, the more slots the model has to store information, so it can remember more patterns and produce more accurate predictions, because each extra slot can encode a different piece of task structure. But a bigger hidden state also means more arithmetic to do with each data point, which makes training slower and uses more compute. A naive attempt is to just train with a small hidden state from the start. This trains faster, but the model cannot hold enough patterns, so accuracy drops, because there are not enough slots to encode all the patterns needed for the task.

The fundamental problem is that we do not know in advance which state dimensions are truly important for a given task. If we could identify and keep only the important ones, we could skip the useless dimensions and save computation without sacrificing quality.

callout.html: The paper identifies which hidden state dimensions matter during training, then removes the rest.

panels.title: 1. Large state, slow training

panels.title: 2. Hankel tells us what matters

panels.title: 3. Drop unimportant dimensions early
panels.caption: Training gradually removes low-influence dimensions, shrinking the state over time.

panels.title: 4. Smaller state, faster training

steps.text: Initialize the model with a large hidden state to capture all possible patterns.
For each state dimension, compute a Hankel singular value (a score of how much that dimension contributes to the model's output).
Sort dimensions from highest to lowest influence score.
Gradually remove dimensions with low Hankel singular values, collapsing the hidden state as training progresses.

The final model is smaller and faster because fewer dimensions means fewer numbers to multiply, and it has preserved the patterns that matter because you kept the high-influence dimensions that learned task structure.

paras: The paper modifies the hidden state dimensions themselves — specifically, which dimensions are kept during training. Most machine learning papers change weights (the numbers that control how the model processes data) or gradients (the signals that guide how to update those numbers). This paper is different: it changes the state dimension structure itself, keeping some and removing others based on their computed influence score.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: Hankel singular value
hidden.name: Hankel singular value
paras: A Hankel singular value is a score from control theory that measures how much a state dimension influences the model's output. The name comes from the Hankel matrix, a mathematical tool used to analyze dynamical systems (systems that change over time). To compute it: the model collects inputs and outputs over a window of time, stacks them into a matrix, and then factorizes that matrix to find which components matter most. A high Hankel singular value means that dimension carries important information and changing it would alter the output noticeably. A low value means the dimension is nearly redundant.

The paper applies Hankel singular value analysis during training. At regular intervals (or at each training step), it computes which state dimensions have low influence and marks them for removal. The model gradually shrinks as training proceeds, shedding dimensions that the data has determined are not needed for this particular task.

heat.caption: Darker means higher Hankel singular value (more influence on output); highlighted dims are typically kept.

reads.html: Hankel singular value tells you how much each piece of the hidden state contributes to what the model predicts. High values mean the dimension is important; low values mean it can be removed without hurting accuracy.

Control theory uses Hankel matrices to analyze linear time-invariant systems; balanced truncation theory guarantees that removing low Hankel singular value dimensions preserves input-output behavior with bounded error.

mechanism.h2: Why in-training compression works better than shrinking from the start
paras: The mechanism hinges on learning stages. When you start training, the model does not yet know which patterns matter for your task. A large hidden state lets every dimension explore and test different behaviors. As training progresses, most dimensions gravitate toward either holding important patterns or becoming nearly inactive. By measuring influence via Hankel singular values and removing the inactive dimensions, the model sheds dead weight while keeping the dimensions that have already found task-critical patterns, because those dimensions have already been sculpted by gradient updates into shapes that solve the task.

In contrast, if you train with a small hidden state from the start, you never give those task-critical patterns a chance to develop in the first place. The model is constrained so early that it cannot capture the full expressivity of the problem. The compressed model trained in-training preserves structure that a small model would have had to rediscover or relearn.

There is also a practical efficiency win: early training steps are cheap (the large state is searching), but as dimensions are pruned, later steps get cheaper too. The model accelerates as it converges, because the computationally expensive part (large state math) shrinks over time.

stages.s: Raw sequence (e.g., stock prices over time)
Large hidden state captures all possible patterns
Compute Hankel singular values for each dimension
Remove dimensions with low influence scores
Compressed model: smaller state, preserved task patterns

math.h2: The equation: Hankel singular value decomposition
math.words: Hankel singular value = the magnitude of a singular value from the factorization of a Hankel matrix (a matrix built from system inputs and outputs over time). Dimensions are ranked by their singular values and low-rank dimensions are pruned.
math.equation: H = [y(1) y(2) ... y(m); y(2) y(3) ... y(m+1); ...; y(p) y(p+1) ... y(p+m-1)] = U * Sigma * V^T; keep dimensions where Sigma_i > threshold
symbols: Hankel matrix (rows and columns built from outputs over different time windows)
orthogonal matrices from factorization (describes the principal directions)
diagonal matrix of singular values (the importance scores)
the ith singular value (score for dimension i)
cutoff: keep dimensions above this score, remove below

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose we have a 4-dimensional hidden state. Hankel analysis produces singular values: [8.2, 5.1, 1.3, 0.4].
We set threshold = 2.0 (remove any dimension scoring below 2.0).
Result: keep dimensions 1 (score 8.2) and 2 (score 5.1); remove dimensions 3 (score 1.3) and 4 (score 0.4).
New hidden state size: 2 dimensions. Later layers and matrix multiplications are 2x faster. Training accelerates.

math.note: Hankel singular values come from control theory's balanced truncation, which guarantees that removing low-score dimensions preserves the system's input-output behavior with a bounded error margin.

charts.title: Small model trained from start
charts.note: Fast to train, but too small to learn all patterns; accuracy suffers.

charts.title: This paper: in-training compression
charts.note: Slightly longer training because early large-state steps cost more compute, but pruning saves time later. Accuracy much better because the model had room to learn all task patterns before shrinking.

items.html: If you remove dimensions before the model has finished learning task-critical patterns, you cut off important structure prematurely. The model then cannot recover that lost expressivity. Solution: prune gradually over training, not all at once.

If the Hankel singular value threshold is too high, you remove dimensions that were actually important but had not yet ramped up in influence. If too low, you keep too much dead weight and do not save compute. The threshold should be tuned to the problem and learned over time.

items.b: Hankel matrix built from insufficient data.
items.html: The Hankel matrix must be constructed from a long enough sequence of outputs to capture the system's true behavior. If the window is too short, the singular values will be noisy and unreliable, leading to bad pruning decisions.

Start with a large state, compute Hankel singular values regularly, prune gradually (a small fraction of dimensions per epoch), and stop pruning once the state reaches your target size. This works because the model first explores and finds all patterns, then pruning removes only dead dimensions, leaving learned structure intact and training speedier as fewer numbers need updating.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple synthetic time-series task (e.g., predicting the next value in a noisy periodic signal, or forecasting from a simple dynamical system). Train three models: (1) a small State Space Model, (2) a large model with no pruning, and (3) a large model with in-training compression using Hankel singular value pruning. Measure both the final task accuracy and the total training time (CPU or GPU minutes). The demo should show that the compressed model achieves accuracy closer to the large-no-pruning model while training nearly as fast as the small model.
demo.metric_eq: accuracy = (correct_predictions / total_predictions); training_time = total_seconds; speedup = training_time_large_unpruned / training_time_compressed
demo.closing: The demo must make it impossible to miss that in-training compression outpaces both small training (lower accuracy) and large training (slower speed) by finding a middle ground: start large to learn all patterns, shrink during training to save compute.
